passage: I'm Shalini, and Rafiq has sat next to me since class one. He used to love maths, shouting "Got it!" across the room. Now, at sixteen, he's different. In our study group he stares at the first question for ages, then scrolls his phone, then stares again. "If I start and it's not perfect, what's the point?" he muttered once. He told me he'd been up till two most nights. Last week he topped the unit test with 96. Everyone clapped. He just shrugged. "Should have been a hundred." At lunch he went back to the classroom to redo the paper. I don't know exactly what's going on inside him. But I miss the boy who shouted "Got it!"

qa.q: What mark did Rafiq get in the unit test?
qa.a: He topped the unit test with 96.

qa.q: What does Rafiq's "Should have been a hundred" suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels empty rather than happy, as if even a top mark is not good enough.

qa.q: What choice keeps trapping Rafiq, and what might help him out of it?
qa.a: He delays starting because the work might not be perfect, so he stays up late; a rough first try and a talk with a trusted adult could loosen the fear.

qa.q: How does Shalini seem to feel about the change in Rafiq?
qa.a: Shalini seems sad and worried, missing the old Rafiq who used to enjoy maths.

grounding: A classmate describes a sixteen-year-old who puts off work from dread, feels flat after a top mark and has lost his joy in maths.

passage:
Two weeks before the deadline: Hrithik had a chemistry project due and a blank file. Every time he opened it, his chest tightened: what if it wasn't the best in class? He reorganised his desk instead, three times.
The night before: He worked until four, redoing the title page twice. Ritu messaged, "Sleep, genius." He didn't reply.
Results day: Full marks. Ritu hugged him in the corridor. "You did it!" Hrithik smiled for her sake, but felt oddly flat. On the walk home he was already thinking, the next one has to be even better. He used to love mixing solutions in the lab. He couldn't remember the last time it had felt fun.

qa.q: How many times did Hrithik reorganise his desk?
qa.a: He reorganised it three times.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel after getting full marks, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt flat rather than happy; he smiled for Ritu's sake but was already thinking the next one had to be better.

qa.q: What choice in the first two weeks made the project harder?
qa.a: Reorganising his desk instead of starting, out of fear, left him working until four the night before.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel if she noticed Hrithik smiling only for her sake?
qa.a: She would probably feel worried that Hrithik can't enjoy his own success.

grounding: A teenager delays out of dread, works through the night, feels empty after full marks and finds the bar has moved higher again.

passage: The history project was due Monday, and on Saturday Damini still hadn't started. Every time she opened a blank document, her chest tightened: what if it wasn't the best in class, like last time? Then the power went out across the colony, and with it the laptop battery. By candlelight she panicked, writing and crossing out till two in the morning. On Monday she submitted it, exhausted. On Friday the result came: 19 out of 20, the highest in class. Her friend Sonali squealed and hugged her. Damini smiled for the photo, but on the walk home she felt nothing, only a flat, grey tiredness, and one thought: next time, it has to be 20.

qa.q: What mark did Damini get?
qa.a: 19 out of 20, the highest in class.

qa.q: How did Damini feel on the walk home?
qa.a: She felt empty and flat, with no joy, already raising the bar to 20.

qa.q: What could help Damini before the next project?
qa.a: Starting with a rough draft early and talking to a trusted adult about how the pressure feels.

qa.q: How might Sonali see Damini's result?
qa.a: Sonali is thrilled for her, not seeing the empty feeling behind Damini's smile.

grounding: Shows a teen who delays from dread, works late in a panic and feels empty after a top result as the standard rises.

passage: At the tuition centre in Hyderabad, Kishore got his mock board result: 96 in physics. Farida-ma'am read it out, and the class clapped. Kishore nodded and went back to his seat. Two months ago, 90 would have made him dance. Now he was already counting the four marks he'd lost. That night he sat at his desk from nine to two, not studying, just opening the chemistry book and closing it, too scared to begin in case he couldn't do it perfectly. At breakfast his little sister asked why he never played carrom any more. He didn't have an answer. He used to love chemistry. Now it felt like a test he was always about to fail.

qa.q: What did Kishore score in physics?
What was Kishore feeling when he kept opening and closing the chemistry book?
qa.a: He was scared of not doing it perfectly, so fear stopped him even starting.

qa.q: How could Farida-ma'am or his family help Kishore?
qa.a: Notice the pressure, talk with him about it, and help him rediscover enjoyment rather than only marks.

qa.q: What is it like for his little sister when Kishore stops playing carrom?
qa.a: She probably misses him and feels confused about why he has changed.

grounding: Illustrates a teen whose rising standards lead to late nights, dread-driven delay and loss of joy.

passage:
"You got the scholarship, Thomas! Why aren't you celebrating?"
"I don't know, Manoj. It felt good for about ten seconds."
"Ten seconds? I'd be dancing on the roof for a week."
"The next round is harder. If I don't get top ten there, what was the point of this one?"
"You've been saying that since Class 8. First it was the school prize, then the district, now this."
Thomas picked at the label on his water bottle. "I haven't even started the next essay. Every time I open it, I just can't."
"Because you don't know what to write?"
"Because what if it's not good enough."
Manoj was quiet. "Remember when we used to do science club stuff just for fun? You loved that."
"Yeah." Thomas looked out of the window. "I miss that."

qa.q: How long did the scholarship feel good for Thomas?
qa.a: About ten seconds.

qa.q: Why hasn't Thomas started the next essay?
qa.a: He is afraid it won't be good enough, so dread stops him beginning.

qa.q: What could Manoj suggest to help Thomas?
qa.a: Doing something just for fun again, and talking to a teacher or parent about the pressure.

qa.q: How does Manoj see Thomas's pattern?
qa.a: Manoj sees the goal keep moving since Class 8 and misses the old, fun-loving Thomas.

grounding: Shows a teen who feels little after success, delays from fear, and whose standards keep rising while joy fades.

passage:
Last term I got 96 in the chemistry exam. Everyone clapped. I felt nothing. Just: why not 100?
Looking back, that was when studying stopped being fun. Before, I liked chemistry. I used to draw molecules in my notebook for no reason. Then every test became a test of whether I was good enough.
The funny thing is, I didn't even study more. I sat at my desk till midnight, scared to start, scrolling and tidying. Then I'd cram in panic at two a.m.
Arohi asked me once, "Aren't you happy with 96?" I said, "It was a lucky paper." She looked at me like I was a stranger.
I'm trying something now. When I get a mark, I write one thing I enjoyed learning before I let myself look at the number.
Ujjwal

qa.q: What mark did Ujjwal get in the chemistry exam?
How did Ujjwal feel after getting 96, and why?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt empty, feeling nothing but "why not 100?", because the standard kept moving higher.

qa.q: What is Ujjwal trying now, and why might it help?
qa.a: Writing one thing Ujjwal enjoyed learning before looking at the mark, which may bring back some joy and loosen the grip of the number.

qa.q: How might Arohi have felt when Ujjwal called it "a lucky paper"?
qa.a: Arohi seemed surprised and a bit worried, looking at Ujjwal like a stranger, since a 96 seemed worth being happy about.

grounding: Shows a teen whose rising standards bring late-night dread, procrastination and emptiness after a good result, with joy draining from learning.
